subTopicTitle: Constitutional Framework: 97th CAA 2011, Article 19(1)(c), Article 43B, and Part IX-B

prelimsCapsule.coreConceptSummary: The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011, granted constitutional status and protection to cooperative societies in India, inserting a new Fundamental Right, a Directive Principle of State Policy, and a new Part in the Constitution to promote their democratic, autonomous, and professional functioning. However, its federal implications were significantly altered by a 2021 Supreme Court judgment.
highYieldFacts: The 97th CAA came into effect on February 15, 2012.
It inserted Article 19(1)(c), making the 'right to form cooperative societies' a Fundamental Right.
It added Article 43B as a Directive Principle of State Policy, obligating states to promote cooperatives.
It inserted Part IX-B (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT), laying down provisions for the management, audit, and elections of cooperative societies.

The Supreme Court, in *Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021)*, struck down Part IX-B in relation to state cooperative societies for lacking ratification by states under Article 368(2) proviso, but upheld its application to multi-state cooperative societies and the validity of Articles 19(1)(c) and 43B.
trapsAndElimination: Confusing the scope of Part IX-B after the 2021 Supreme Court judgment (valid for multi-state, invalid for state cooperatives).
Misattributing the DPSP for cooperatives as an enforceable right or vice-versa with the Fundamental Right.
Assuming the 97th CAA fully uniformized cooperative governance across all types of cooperatives post-2021 judgment.

mainsFramework.inDepthTheoryHtml:
I. Introduction to Cooperative Societies and their Constitutional Journey

Cooperative societies represent a unique form of organization where individuals voluntarily come together for their economic and social betterment through joint action. Rooted in principles of self-help, self-responsibility, democracy, equality, and solidarity, cooperatives have played a significant role in India's rural economy, particularly in sectors like agriculture, dairy, credit, and housing. Before the 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011, cooperative societies were primarily governed by state-level legislations, leading to inconsistencies, political interference, and operational inefficiencies across states. The absence of a uniform constitutional framework hindered their autonomous and democratic functioning, often leading to their dormancy or mismanagement.

II. The Rationale Behind the 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011

The need for a constitutional framework arose from the persistent challenges faced by the cooperative sector, including:

  • Lack of Uniformity: Disparate state laws resulted in varying standards of governance and regulation.
  • Political Interference: Frequent supersession of elected boards by state governments, undermining democratic control.
  • Operational Inefficiencies: Lack of professional management, accountability, and transparency.
  • Financial Weakness: Inadequate audit mechanisms and financial discipline.

The 97th CAA aimed to provide constitutional sanctity, protect the autonomy of cooperatives, ensure their democratic functioning, and promote professional management to revitalize the sector.

III. Key Provisions Introduced by the 97th CAA

The Amendment made three significant insertions into the Constitution:

  • Article 19(1)(c): Right to form Cooperative Societies as a Fundamental Right: This amendment elevated the right to form cooperative societies to the status of a Fundamental Right, ensuring that citizens have the constitutional liberty to establish and operate cooperative ventures. This aligns cooperatives with other fundamental rights of association, strengthening their democratic foundation.
  • Article 43B: Promotion of Cooperative Societies as a Directive Principle of State Policy (DPSP): This new DPSP mandates that the State shall endeavour to promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control, and professional management of cooperative societies. While not justiciable, it serves as a guiding principle for state policy formulation, reflecting the constitutional vision for the sector.
  • Part IX-B: The Cooperative Societies (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT): This comprehensive new Part lays down detailed provisions to govern cooperative societies. Key aspects include:
    • Incorporation: Mandatory state legislation for incorporation, regulation, and winding up.
    • Board of Directors: Specifies a maximum of 21 directors, with reservation for two women members and one Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe member.
    • Term of Office: A fixed term of five years for elected members of the board.
    • Elections: Mandatory and timely elections to be conducted by a State Election Commission or a similar body before the expiry of the board's term.
    • Audit: Mandatory audit of accounts within six months of the close of the financial year.
    • General Body Meetings: Mandatory holding of annual general body meetings.
    • Supersession and Suspension of Board: Restrictions on supersession or suspension of the board for more than six months, and only on specific grounds (e.g., persistent default, negligence). No supersession if there is no government shareholding or loan.
    • Offences and Penalties: Provisions for penalizing offences related to cooperatives to ensure accountability.

IV. Significance and Intended Impact of 97th CAA

The 97th CAA was hailed for its potential to:

  • Strengthen Grassroots Democracy: By ensuring regular elections and limiting state intervention, it aimed to empower members and foster democratic decision-making.
  • Promote Economic Empowerment: Facilitating self-help initiatives, especially in rural areas, leading to poverty alleviation, improved access to credit, and market linkages for producers.
  • Ensure Professionalism and Accountability: Mandatory audit, timely elections, and limited supersession were designed to bring transparency and efficiency.
  • Reduce Political Interference: Curtailing arbitrary government control over the management of cooperative societies.

V. The Landmark *Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah* (2021) Supreme Court Judgment

Despite its progressive intent, the 97th CAA faced challenges on federal grounds. The Supreme Court, in its 2021 verdict, delivered a crucial interpretation of its validity:

  • Background: The challenge was primarily based on the argument that Part IX-B, dealing extensively with cooperative societies (a state subject under Entry 32 of State List), affected the federal structure of the Constitution and therefore required ratification by at least half of the state legislatures as per the proviso to Article 368(2) of the Constitution.
  • Verdict:
    1. A five-judge bench unanimously upheld the validity of Articles 19(1)(c) and 43B, stating that they do not alter the basic federal structure.
    2. However, by a 2:1 majority, the Court struck down Part IX-B (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT) of the Constitution *insofar as it relates to state cooperative societies*. The majority held that Parliament lacked the legislative competence to enact these provisions for state cooperative societies without the requisite ratification from state legislatures.
    3. The Court clarified that Part IX-B would continue to apply to *multi-state cooperative societies* as Parliament has the legislative competence to make laws concerning such entities.
  • Implications:
    1. Reaffirmation of Federalism: The judgment strongly upheld the federal nature of the Indian Constitution and the sanctity of Article 368(2) proviso, emphasizing that Parliament cannot unilaterally encroach upon state legislative domains.
    2. Restoration of State Autonomy: States regained their full legislative autonomy over state cooperative societies, reinforcing that 'cooperative societies' remains a state subject.
    3. Bifurcated Regulatory Regime: A dual regulatory framework emerged – central law (Part IX-B, as applicable through relevant central acts like Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act) for multi-state cooperatives, and state laws for state-specific cooperatives.
    4. Impact on Uniformity: The judgment significantly undermined the goal of achieving uniform governance standards for all cooperative societies across the nation, leading to potential regulatory fragmentation and varied application of best practices.

VI. Challenges and Way Forward

The judgment, while constitutionally sound, presents challenges. State-level cooperatives might continue to grapple with issues of political interference and lack of professionalism if states do not proactively amend their respective cooperative laws in line with the spirit of the 97th CAA. The way forward involves:

  • State-led Reforms: Encouraging states to voluntarily adopt provisions similar to Part IX-B in their respective state cooperative acts.
  • Strengthening Multi-State Cooperatives: Leveraging the constitutional provisions for multi-state cooperatives to set benchmarks for good governance.
  • Promoting Cooperative Federalism: Facilitating dialogue and consensus between the Centre and states to evolve a common framework for strengthening the cooperative movement while respecting federal divisions of power.

dimensions.constitutional_or_legal: The 97th CAA inserted Articles 19(1)(c), 43B, and Part IX-B, granting constitutional recognition and framework to cooperative societies. The landmark *Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah* (2021) judgment profoundly reinterpreted its federal validity, striking down Part IX-B for state cooperatives due to non-compliance with Article 368(2) proviso, while upholding its application to multi-state cooperatives and the validity of Articles 19(1)(c) and 43B. This reaffirms the federal distribution of legislative powers concerning state subjects.
dimensions.socio_economic: Cooperative societies are crucial for grassroots economic development, poverty alleviation, and empowering marginalized communities. They facilitate access to credit, markets, and resources in agriculture, dairy, fisheries, and housing sectors. The 97th CAA sought to enhance their democratic functioning and efficiency, thereby boosting their socio-economic impact. Post-judgment, the efficacy depends on state-level legislative reforms to continue driving this development.
dimensions.administrative_governance: The 97th CAA aimed to bring in good governance practices through mandatory elections, fixed terms, audit mechanisms, and limits on supersession. The SC judgment, by making Part IX-B inapplicable to state cooperatives, shifts the burden of establishing robust administrative and governance structures back to state legislatures. Effective oversight, transparency, and accountability mechanisms remain crucial for preventing malpractices and ensuring democratic functioning, both at state and multi-state levels.
dimensions.international_or_comparative: The constitutional recognition of cooperative societies aligns India with global best practices articulated by the International Cooperative Alliance (ICA) principles. Many countries promote cooperatives through various legal and policy frameworks. The Indian experience, particularly the federal challenge, offers a unique case study in balancing national aspirations for cooperative development with constitutional federalism, providing insights into legislative design for social and economic institutions in diverse federal polities.

landmarkJudgmentsOrReports: Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021): Supreme Court judgment striking down Part IX-B of the Constitution (related to state cooperative societies) for non-ratification by states under Article 368(2) proviso.

modelMainsQA.modelAnswerHtml:
Cooperative societies, founded on principles of self-help and mutual aid, have been vital for India's socio-economic fabric, particularly in agriculture, dairy, and rural credit. However, prior to 2011, they suffered from political interference, lack of uniformity, and mismanagement. The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011, sought to revitalize this sector by granting constitutional status and protection, introducing:

  • A new Fundamental Right in Article 19(1)(c) to form cooperative societies.
  • A new Directive Principle of State Policy (DPSP) in Article 43B, urging states to promote their autonomous functioning.
  • A new Part IX-B (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT) with detailed provisions for their governance.

Transformative Potential of 97th CAA:

The Amendment harboured significant potential:

  • Enhanced Democratic Functioning: Mandating regular elections for a fixed term (5 years) and limiting arbitrary supersession aimed to curb political control.
  • Promoted Professionalism: Provisions for mandatory audit (within 6 months) and a maximum board size (21, with reservations for women, SC/ST) sought to instill transparency and efficiency.
  • Empowered Members: Elevated the right to form cooperatives to a Fundamental Right, strengthening grassroots participation and self-governance.
  • Socio-Economic Development: Expected to foster self-reliance, rural prosperity, and equitable growth by strengthening cooperatives in critical sectors.

Implications of Supreme Court's 2021 Judgment:

Despite its promise, the 97th CAA's federal implications were critically examined in Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021). The Supreme Court's verdict had profound implications:

  • Upholding Federalism: The Court struck down Part IX-B insofar as it related to state cooperative societies, citing that Parliament lacked the power to legislate on a state subject without ratification by at least half of the state legislatures as mandated by Article 368(2) proviso. This decisively reaffirmed the federal distribution of powers.
  • Bifurcated Regulatory Regime: Part IX-B remains valid for multi-state cooperative societies, for which Parliament has legislative competence. This creates a dual regulatory framework, where state cooperatives continue to be governed by diverse state laws.
  • Impact on Uniformity: The judgment undermined the original intent of bringing uniformity and robust governance standards across all cooperatives. State cooperatives are now reliant on respective state governments to adopt similar reformative measures.
  • Validation of FR and DPSP: Articles 19(1)(c) and 43B were unanimously upheld, as they do not impinge on the federal structure, thus maintaining the constitutional recognition and guiding principles for cooperatives.

Challenges and Way Forward:

The judgment, while constitutionally sound, poses challenges to ensure consistent good governance in state cooperatives. The way forward necessitates:

  1. State-led Legislative Reforms: States must proactively amend their cooperative laws to incorporate democratic and transparent provisions aligned with the spirit of the 97th CAA.
  2. Strengthening Multi-State Framework: Leveraging the Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act to drive best practices and foster accountability.
  3. Cooperative Federalism: Encouraging dialogue between the Centre and states to evolve a common vision for the cooperative sector, promoting a balance between state autonomy and the national interest in cooperative development.

In conclusion, the 97th CAA marked a significant constitutional step, yet the Supreme Court's ruling underscores the intricate balance of federalism. The onus now shifts to states to champion reforms, ensuring that the transformative potential of the cooperative movement is fully realized within India's federal democratic framework.

practiceMCQs.question:
With reference to the 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011, consider the following statements:
1. It inserted Article 19(1)(c), making the 'right to form cooperative societies' a Fundamental Right.
2. It introduced Part IX-B to the Constitution, providing for democratic control and professional management of cooperative societies.
3. The Supreme Court in 2021 struck down the entire 97th CAA as unconstitutional due to lack of state ratification.
practiceMCQs.explanation: Statement 1 is correct. The 97th CAA indeed inserted Article 19(1)(c), granting Fundamental Right status to forming cooperative societies. Statement 2 is correct. Part IX-B was introduced to provide a constitutional framework for the governance of cooperative societies. Statement 3 is incorrect. The Supreme Court in *Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021)* did not strike down the *entire* 97th CAA. It upheld Articles 19(1)(c) and 43B, and only struck down Part IX-B *insofar as it related to state cooperative societies* due to the lack of state ratification under Article 368(2) proviso. It explicitly stated that Part IX-B would continue to apply to multi-state cooperative societies.

practiceMCQs.question: Which of the following provisions of the 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011, continues to be applicable to 'state cooperative societies' even after the Supreme Court's judgment in *Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021)*?
options: (a) The fixed term of five years for the board of directors.
(b) The mandatory audit of accounts within six months of the financial year closure.
(c) The right to form cooperative societies as a Fundamental Right.
(d) The restriction on supersession of the board for more than six months.
practiceMCQs.explanation: The Supreme Court in *Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021)* explicitly struck down Part IX-B (which contains provisions for fixed terms, mandatory audit, and restrictions on supersession) insofar as it related to state cooperative societies. Therefore, options (a), (b), and (d) are no longer constitutionally binding for state cooperative societies. However, the Court unanimously upheld Article 19(1)(c), which makes the 'right to form cooperative societies' a Fundamental Right, and Article 43B (DPSP). Hence, the right to form cooperative societies as a Fundamental Right (Option c) continues to be applicable.
